questions.prompt: On an op-amp's open-loop Bode plot, the unity-gain frequency \(\omega_u\) is
options: the \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency of the open-loop gain
the frequency at which \(|A(j\omega)|=1\) (0 dB)
the frequency at which the phase reaches \(-180^\circ\)
the frequency at which \(|A|\) has dropped to half its DC value
questions.explanation:
\(\omega_u\) is where the open-loop magnitude crosses 0 dB (reader Eq. 17.19). For a single-pole op-amp, \(\omega_u\approx A_0\,\omega_{-3dB}\), which is why it is also called the gain-bandwidth product.
• The \(-3\) dB frequency is the (much lower) dominant pole.
• A single pole never reaches \(-180^\circ\).
• Half the DC gain is the \(-6\) dB point, near the pole.

questions.prompt: Closing a feedback loop around a single-pole op-amp with DC loop gain \(T_0\) does what to the DC gain and the bandwidth?
options: Divides the gain by \(1+T_0\) and multiplies the bandwidth by \(1+T_0\), so gain × bandwidth is unchanged
Multiplies both the gain and the bandwidth by \(1+T_0\)
Divides both the gain and the bandwidth by \(1+T_0\)
Leaves the bandwidth unchanged and lowers the gain
questions.explanation: From \(G_{CL}=\dfrac{A_0/(1+T_0)}{1+j\omega\tau/(1+T_0)}\) (reader Eq. 17.26), the DC gain falls by \(1+T_0\) and the pole moves up by \(1+T_0\). Their product, the gain-bandwidth, stays at \(\approx\omega_u\): you can trade gain for bandwidth but not get both.

questions.prompt: An op-amp has DC gain \(A_0=10^5\) (100 dB) and a dominant pole at \(f_{-3dB}=10\ \mathrm{Hz}\). What is its unity-gain frequency \(f_u\), in MHz?
questions.explanation:
\(f_u\approx A_0\,f_{-3dB}=10^5\times10\ \mathrm{Hz}=10^6\ \mathrm{Hz}=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\) (reader Eq. 17.21).
On the Bode plot: 100 dB must be lost at 20 dB/decade, i.e. 5 decades above 10 Hz.

questions.prompt: An op-amp with \(f_u=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\) is used in a non-inverting amplifier with gain 20 (\(f=0.05\)). What is the closed-loop bandwidth, in kHz?
questions.explanation:
Closed-loop bandwidth \(\approx f\cdot f_u=0.05\times10\ \mathrm{MHz}=500\ \mathrm{kHz}\) (reader Eq. 17.27–17.29).
Check: gain × bandwidth \(=20\times500\ \mathrm{kHz}=10\ \mathrm{MHz}=f_u\). Common mistake: dividing \(f_u\) by \(1+20\).

questions.prompt: An op-amp has \(f_u=5\ \mathrm{MHz}\) and a dominant pole at 20 Hz. What is its open-loop gain magnitude \(|A|\) at 50 kHz?
questions.explanation:
Far above the pole, \(A(j\omega)\approx\dfrac{\omega_u}{j\omega}\) (reader Eq. 17.22), so \(|A|\approx\dfrac{f_u}{f}=\dfrac{5\ \mathrm{MHz}}{50\ \mathrm{kHz}}=100\).
Exact: \(A_0=f_u/f_p=2.5\times10^5\) and \(|A|=\dfrac{A_0}{\sqrt{1+(50000/20)^2}}=100\). The open-loop gain at signal frequencies can be far below the datasheet's DC gain.

questions.prompt: A unity-gain follower (\(f=1\)) uses an op-amp with unity-gain frequency \(f_u\). What is the closed-loop bandwidth?
options: About \(f_u/2\)
The op-amp's open-loop \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency
Infinite, since the gain is 1
About \(f_u\): the follower uses the full gain-bandwidth
questions.explanation:
Closed-loop bandwidth \(\approx f\cdot f_u\), and \(f=1\) for a follower, so the bandwidth is \(\approx f_u\) (reader Sec. 17.5.6 and Fig. 17.18). It is the widest-band configuration because it has the lowest gain.
• \(f_u/2\) is the bandwidth of a gain \(-1\) INVERTING stage (noise gain 2).
• The open-loop pole is \(1+T_0\) times lower.

questions.prompt: A (weak) op-amp has \(A_0=10\) and a single pole at 1 MHz, so \(A_0f_{-3dB}=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\). It is connected as a unity-gain follower. What is the closed-loop \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) bandwidth?
options: 10 MHz
1 MHz
11 MHz
0.91 MHz
questions.explanation:
Exactly, the pole moves to \((1+T_0)f_{-3dB}=(1+10\cdot1)\times1\ \mathrm{MHz}=11\ \mathrm{MHz}\) (reader Eq. 17.27), with DC gain \(10/11=0.909\).
The shortcut 'bandwidth \(=f\cdot f_u\)' assumes \(T_0\gg1\) (it replaces \(1+T_0\) by \(T_0\)); with \(T_0=10\) it is 10% off. Gain × bandwidth is still \(0.909\times11=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\).

questions.prompt: You need a gain of 100. Option 1: one non-inverting stage of gain 100. Option 2: two cascaded stages of gain 10 each. Each op-amp has \(f_u=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\). What is the \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) bandwidth of Option 2, in kHz? (Option 1 gives 100 kHz.)
questions.explanation:
Each gain-10 stage has a single pole at \(f_u/10=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Cascaded, \(|H|=\dfrac{100}{1+(f/1\ \mathrm{MHz})^2}\), which is \(1/\sqrt2\) of its DC value when \(1+(f/f_1)^2=\sqrt2\):
\[f_{-3dB}=f_1\sqrt{\sqrt2-1}=0.6436\times1\ \mathrm{MHz}=643.6\ \mathrm{kHz}\]
Splitting the gain wins a 6.4× wider bandwidth, but NOT the naive 1 MHz: two equal poles each contribute \(-1.5\ \mathrm{dB}\) at \(0.64f_1\). Common mistake: answering 1000 kHz.

questions.prompt: An OTA (no output buffer) with internal capacitance \(C_x\) drives a load capacitor \(C_L=4C_x\) directly. How does its gain-bandwidth product compare with the unloaded value \(G_m/C_x\)?
options: It is unchanged; the GBW depends only on \(G_m\) and \(C_x\)
It drops by a factor of 5, to \(G_m/(C_x+C_L)\)
It drops by a factor of 4
It increases by a factor of 5
questions.explanation:
Without a buffer, the load capacitance sits in parallel with \(C_x\) at the high-impedance node, so the pole becomes \(\dfrac{1}{R_x(C_x+C_L)}\) (reader Eq. 17.18; the printed form '\(\frac{1}{R_x}(C_x+C_L)\)' is missing parentheses). The DC gain \(G_mR_x\) is unchanged, so GBW \(=\dfrac{G_m}{C_x+C_L}=\dfrac{G_m}{5C_x}\).
• 'Unchanged' would be true with an ideal buffer isolating \(C_L\).
• The total is \(C_x+4C_x=5C_x\), not \(4C_x\).

questions.prompt: Preview of closed-loop frequency response. An inverting amplifier with \(R_2/R_1=9\) uses an op-amp with \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Its closed-loop response is one-pole with the pole at \(f_u/(1+R_2/R_1)\). What is \(|v_o/v_s|\) at 300 kHz?
questions.explanation:
Closed-loop pole: \(\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{MHz}}{1+9}=100\ \mathrm{kHz}\) (the 'noise gain' \(1+R_2/R_1=1/f\) sets it, not \(R_2/R_1\)).
\(|H|=\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{1+(300/100)^2}}=\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{10}}=2.846\).
The op-amp frequency-response skill applies this to real inverting and non-inverting amplifiers.

questions.prompt: Preview of amplifier compensation. An op-amp has \(A_0=10^5\), a dominant pole at 100 Hz (so \(f_u=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\)) and a second pole at 5 MHz. With \(f=0.1\) the loop gain \(T=Af\) crosses unity near \(f\cdot f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\). What is the phase of \(T\) at 1 MHz, in degrees?
questions.explanation:
\(\angle T=-\tan^{-1}\!\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{MHz}}{100\ \mathrm{Hz}}-\tan^{-1}\!\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{MHz}}{5\ \mathrm{MHz}}=-89.99^\circ-11.31^\circ=-101.3^\circ\).
The loop is about \(79^\circ\) away from \(-180^\circ\) where \(|T|=1\): that margin is what the stability skill calls phase margin. Lowering the gain toward a follower (\(f=1\)) pushes the crossover up toward the 5 MHz pole and eats the margin.

questions.prompt: Preview of slew rate. A follower built from an op-amp with \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\) responds to a small step linearly: \(v_o(t)=V_i(1-e^{-\omega_ut})\). For a \(V_i=1\ \mathrm{V}\) step, what initial slope \(dv_o/dt\) would the linear model demand?
options: \(6.28\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\)
\(1\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\)
\(0.159\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\)
\(62.8\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\)
questions.explanation:
The follower's time constant is \(\tau=1/\omega_u\) (bandwidth = full GBW). The initial slope is \(V_i\,\omega_u=1\ \mathrm{V}\times2\pi\times10^6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}=6.28\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\) (reader Eq. 18.20).
• \(1\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\) forgets the \(2\pi\).
• \(0.159\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\) divides by \(2\pi\) instead.
If the op-amp's maximum slew rate is below this, the output ramps at the slew rate instead: the next skills explain when that happens.
questions.figure_alt: Step input and the exponential output of a follower.
